title: Random Numbers
summary: Create **one** random engine, **seed** it once, and use a **distribution** to turn its output into numbers in the range you want. Never create a new engine each time you need a number.
markdown:
## Computers cannot be random A computer follows instructions exactly, so it cannot roll a real die. What it can do is run a formula whose output **looks** random: each number is calculated from the one before. These are called **pseudo-random** numbers. Because every number depends on the previous one, the starting value decides the whole sequence. That starting value is the **seed**. ## Three parts ```mermaid flowchart LR SEED["Seed
where to start"] --> ENG["Engine
std::mt19937
produces raw numbers"] ENG --> DIST["Distribution
shapes them into a range"] DIST --> OUT["4"] ``` | Part | Job | Like | |---|---|---| | **Seed** | The starting point of the sequence | Shuffling a deck | | **Engine** | Produces a long stream of raw, random-looking numbers | The shuffled deck | | **Distribution** | Converts raw numbers into what you asked for, such as 1 to 6 | The rules for reading a card | ## The code ```cpp #include #include int main() { std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; // one engine, seeded once std::uniform_int_distribution die{ 1, 6 }; // 1 to 6, both included for (int i{ 0 }; i < 10; ++i) { std::cout << die(rng) << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } ``` | Piece | What it is | |---|---| | `std::mt19937` | A well-tested engine (the "Mersenne Twister") | | `std::random_device{}()` | Asks the operating system for an unpredictable seed | | `std::uniform_int_distribution{ 1, 6 }` | Whole numbers from 1 to 6, each equally likely | | `die(rng)` | Draw one number: the distribution takes what it needs from the engine | ### Other distributions | Distribution | Produces | |---|---| | `std::uniform_real_distribution{ 0.0, 1.0 }` | Decimals from 0 up to, but not including, 1 | | `std::bernoulli_distribution{ 0.5 }` | `true` or `false`, here with a 50% chance | | `std::normal_distribution{ 170.0, 10.0 }` | A bell curve centred on 170 | ## The same seed gives the same sequence ``` seed 42 gives 17, 3, 88, 41, ... seed 42 gives 17, 3, 88, 41, ... identical seed 99 gives 62, 9, 14, 77, ... ``` This is a feature. A fixed seed makes a "random" program repeatable, which is exactly what you need when testing or chasing a bug. ```cpp std::mt19937 testRng{ 42 }; // same numbers on every run ``` | You want | Seed with | |---|---| | Different results on every run (a game) | `std::random_device{}()` | | Identical results on every run (a test) | a fixed number | ## One engine for the whole program > [!danger] Do not create an engine inside the function that uses it > ```cpp > int roll() > { > std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; // a new engine on every call > return std::uniform_int_distribution{ 1, 6 }(rng); > } > ``` > This throws away the engine after one number. It is slow, and you lose the quality the engine is designed to give over a long sequence. The usual solution is a small header that every file shares: ```cpp // random.h #pragma once #include namespace Random { inline std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; inline int get(int min, int max) { return std::uniform_int_distribution{ min, max }(rng); } } ``` ```cpp int roll{ Random::get(1, 6) }; ``` The engine is created once, when the program starts, and every call to `Random::get` draws from it. The `namespace` and `inline` keywords are explained in the next two lessons. > [!warning] You will see `rand()` in old code > `std::rand() % 6 + 1` is the method inherited from C. Its numbers are of poor quality and slightly favour some results. Recognise it; do not write it.
ideas:
1. Roll two dice ten times and print each total.
2. Flip a coin 1000 times and count heads and tails.
3. Seed an engine with `42` and print five numbers. Run it twice and compare.

cards.a: The engine is designed to produce a long, good-quality sequence from one starting point. Re-seeding restarts it and wastes time.
Whole numbers from 1 to 6 inclusive, each equally likely.

cards.q: Why would you ever want a fixed seed?
cards.a: It makes the program produce the same "random" numbers on every run, so tests and bugs can be repeated.
The numbers come from a formula. They look random but are completely determined by the seed.
